content: Bisulfide, also known as hydrosulfide, refers to the anion with the chemical formula HS−, which is often written as SH−. This anion is the conjugate base of hydrogen sulfide (H2S). In aqueous solutions, the dominant species depends on the pH of the solution. At a pH below 7, hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is the predominant form, while at a pH above 7, bisulfide (HS−) becomes the dominant species. Various salts of bisulfide are well-documented, including sodium hydrosulfide (NaHS), potassium hydrosulfide (KHS), and ammonium hydrosulfide (NH4HS). Some compounds that are nominally described as salts of the sulfide dianion (S2−) are, in reality, primarily composed of hydrosulfide. For instance, the hydrated form of sodium sulfide, which is typically represented as Na2S·(H2O)9, is more accurately described as NaSH·NaOH·(H2O)8. In aqueous solutions, bisulfide absorbs light in the ultraviolet-visible (UV/Vis) spectrum at approximately 230 nm. Researchers have utilized field spectrometers to continuously measure the absorption caused by bisulfide, which allows for the determination of its concentration in environments such as the ocean and sewage systems. It is important to note that bisulfide (HS−) is sometimes mistakenly confused with the disulfide dianion (S22−), which is a chemically distinct species.
